# Diarrhea

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Gastroenterology > Clinical problems > Diarrhea*

[Original Article Link](/library/6M0jpg)

---

## Summary

Diarrhea, defined as three or more loose stools per day or more frequent stool passage than is normal for the individual, is a common disease with a monthly <u>prevalence</u> of around 5% in the United States. <u>Acute diarrhea</u> lasts 14 days or less and is almost always caused by an infectious agent, typically a <u>virus</u>. Testing is seldom required, as the disease tends to be <u>self-limited</u> and care is primarily supportive. <u>Persistent diarrhea</u>, lasting 15–30 days, is also typically caused by an infectious agent, but stool testing for pathogens is generally warranted to confirm the diagnosis. <u>Chronic diarrhea</u>, defined as diarrhea lasting longer than 30 days, has an extensive differential diagnosis. A thorough history followed by systematic stool and blood testing is required to identify the specific etiology. The presence of any <u>red flags</u> for severe or rapidly progressing diarrheal disease (e.g., <u>sepsis</u>, extreme <u>dehydration</u>, blood in the stool) mandates escalation of testing and, in some cases, <u>empiric antibiotics for bacterial gastroenteritis</u>. Ensuring adequate oral hydration, correcting <u>dehydration</u>, and providing symptomatic relief are fundamental components in the care of all patients with diarrhea. Curative treatment is directed toward the underlying cause.

---

For etiologies of acute, persistent, or <u>chronic diarrhea</u>, see specific subsections below.

## Classification

Diarrhea is often classified as watery, fatty, and/or inflammatory to facilitate diagnosis and management. This classification scheme is most relevant for the approach to <u>chronic diarrhea</u>.




| <br>Classification of diarrhea by functional pathology [[10]](/library/7Mc4J10)[[11]](/library/HMcKJ10)[[12]](/library/Sncys10)<br> |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  |  | Pathophysiology | Associated disorders |
| Inflammatory diarrhea |  | <br><br>* Damage to the intestinal <u>mucosa</u> may cause <u>cytokine</u>-induced water hypersecretion, impair absorption of osmotically active substances or fat, and/or disrupt water and <u>electrolyte</u> absorption.<br><br>* Mucus, blood, and <u>leukocytes</u> present in the stool.<br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Ulcerative colitis</u>, <u>Crohn disease</u><br><br>* <u>Colorectal cancer</u><br><br>* Infections<br><br>* <u>Shigellosis</u> (<u>bacillary dysentery</u>)<br><br>* Nontyphoidal: <u>salmonellosis</u><br><br>* <u>Enteroinvasive Escherichia coli</u>, <u>enterohemorrhagic E. coli</u> (<u>O157:H7</u>)<br><br>* <u>Campylobacteriosis</u><br><br>* <u>Yersiniosis</u><br><br>* <u>Amebiasis</u> (<u>amebic dysentery</u> caused by <u>Entamoeba histolytica</u>)<br><br>* <u>Clostridioides difficile</u> (rarely bloody)<br><br><br> |
| Fatty diarrhea | <u>Malabsorption</u> | <br>* Alterations of the intestinal <u>mucosa</u> → impaired absorption of digested food<br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Malabsorption</u> disorders or history of <u>ileal</u> resection<br><br>* Infections<br><br>* <u>Giardiasis</u><br><br>* <u>Small intestinal bacterial overgrowth</u> (<u>SIBO</u>)<br><br>* <u>Tropical sprue</u><br><br>* <u>Whipple disease</u><br><br>* <u>Amyloidosis</u><br><br><br> |
| <u>Maldigestion</u> | <br>* Lack of digestive enzymes → impaired breakdown of food in the intestinal lumen → <u>malabsorption</u> of <u>carbohydrates</u>, <u>proteins</u>, fats, <u>fat-soluble vitamins</u> (A, D, E, K), and <u>vitamin B<sub>12</sub></u><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Exocrine pancreatic insufficiency</u><br><br>* <u>Bile acid diarrhea</u><br><br><br> |  |
| Watery diarrhea | Secretory diarrhea | <br>* Active secretion of water  into the intestinal lumen via inhibition or activation of enzymes (e.g., ↑ <u>cAMP</u> activity)<br><br> | <br><br>* Neuroendocrine disorders, e.g.:<br><br>* <u>Carcinoid syndrome</u><br><br>* <u>Gastrinoma</u><br><br>* Endocrine disorders, e.g.:<br><br>* <u>Hyperthyroidism</u><br><br>* <u>Addison disease</u><br><br>* <u>Diabetes mellitus</u><br><br>* Foodborne infections<br><br>* <u>Cholera</u> (“rice water” diarrhea)<br><br>* <u>Enterotoxigenic E. coli</u> (<u>traveler's diarrhea</u>)<br><br>* <u>C. perfringens</u><br><br>* <u>C. difficile</u> (associated with <u>antibiotic</u> and <u>PPI</u> use)<br><br>* <u>Protozoa</u>: e.g., <u>giardiasis</u>, <u>cryptosporidiosis</u><br><br>* <u>Viruses</u>: e.g., <u>norovirus</u>, <u>rotavirus</u>, <u>adenovirus</u><br><br><br> |
| Osmotic diarrhea | <br>* Poor absorption or excessive ingestion of <u>hydrophilic</u> substances (e.g., salts, sugars, <u>laxatives</u>) causes water to be drawn into the intestinal lumen.<br><br> | <br><br>* Osmotic <u>laxatives</u>: e.g., <u>magnesium citrate</u><br><br>* <u>Carbohydrate malabsorption</u>: e.g., <u>lactose intolerance</u>, <u>fructose intolerance</u> (may also present as <u>fatty diarrhea</u>)<br><br><br> |  |
| <br>Functional diarrheal disorders [[10]](/library/7Mc4J10)<br> | <br>* Rapid intestinal passage due to increased bowel activity<br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Diarrhea-predominant IBS</u> (<u>IBS-D</u>)<br><br>* <u>Functional diarrhea</u>  [[10]](/library/7Mc4J10)[[13]](/library/99cNpe0)<br><br><br> |  |

## Management

### Approach to diarrhea [[11]](/library/HMcKJ10)




* Detailed history and <u>physical examination</u>

* Exclude <u>fecal incontinence</u> and <u>fecal impaction</u>; see “<u>Differential diagnoses of diarrhea</u>.”

* Rule out <u>medication-induced diarrhea</u> and consider <u>factitious diarrhea</u>.

* Classify diarrhea:

* By duration of diarrheal illness: acute, persistent, or chronic

* By clinical presentation: watery, fatty, inflammatory

* Identify any <u>red flags in diarrhea</u> and <u>risk factors</u> for specific causes.

* Review medical and surgical history.

* <u>Supportive care</u>: Start oral hydration (or <u>IV fluids</u>) and offer symptom relief.

* Diagnostics: Obtain only when appropriate.

* Directed therapy: Consider empiric or targeted therapy (e.g., <u>antibiotics</u>) based on clinical presentation and study results.





> [!WARNING]
> Though most patients with diarrhea have mild symptoms and can be managed as outpatients, some patients may present with severe and even life-threatening symptoms that require hospitalization.




> [!TIP]
> In older adults, rule out <u>fecal impaction</u>, which can manifest atypically with <u>paradoxical diarrhea</u> (due to decreased rectal sensation) and nonspecific symptoms (e.g., functional decline, <u>delirium</u>). [[14]](/library/dD0oWR)




> [!TIP]
> <u>Antibiotics</u> should only be utilized for specific indications.




### Clinical assessment of diarrhea [[10]](/library/7Mc4J10)[[12]](/library/Sncys10)




Key features of the disease presentation that facilitate efficient testing and prompt diagnosis include:




* Duration of diarrheal illness

* Acute diarrhea: duration ≤ 14 days

* Persistent diarrhea: duration 15–30 days

* Chronic diarrhea: duration > 30 days

* Stool characteristics: watery, fatty, or bloody stools

* Associated symptoms

* <u>Fever</u>

* Abdominal <u>pain</u> and cramping

* <u>Nausea and vomiting</u> in cases of <u>gastroenteritis</u>

* Signs of <u>dehydration</u>

* Chronic cases: <u>malnutrition</u> and, in children, <u>failure to thrive</u>

* Weight loss

* Defecation urgency, <u>tenesmus</u>, and/or nocturnal symptoms





| Characteristic clinical features in diarrhea according to functional pathology |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| <u>Inflammatory diarrhea</u> |  | <br><br>* Frequent and small volume stools<br><br>* Bloody or <u>purulent</u> stools<br><br>* Abdominal <u>pain</u>, <u>tenesmus</u><br><br>* May be associated with <u>fever</u>, weight loss, fatigue<br><br><br> |  |
| <u>Fatty diarrhea</u> |  | <br><br>* Greasy or oily stools<br><br>* Stools that are difficult to flush<br><br>* Decreases with <u>fasting</u><br><br>* May be associated with weight loss<br><br><br> |  |
| <u>Watery diarrhea</u> | <u>Secretory diarrhea</u> | Loose, watery stools | <br><br>* No change with <u>fasting</u><br><br>* Nocturnal diarrhea present<br><br><br> |
| <u>Functional diarrheal disorders</u> | <br><br>* Decreases with <u>fasting</u><br><br>* Decreased at night<br><br><br> |  |  |
| <u>Osmotic diarrhea</u> | <br><br>* Decreases with <u>fasting</u><br><br>* Decreased at night<br><br>* Food triggers<br><br><br> |  |  |





### Risk factors for diarrhea




Assess for the presence of <u>risk factors</u> for specific etiologies, including:




* Recent travel : associated with <u>traveler's diarrhea</u>

* Occupational or recreational exposure

* May be associated with an infectious <u>disease outbreak</u>

* Potential routes of exposure include:

* Ingestion of contaminated food or beverages at a high-risk event (e.g., picnic, restaurant, buffet)

* Daycare (e.g., in a daycare attendee, family member of attendee, or daycare staff member)

* Direct contact with contaminated surfaces or objects

* Direct contact with an infected individual (e.g., shaking hands, sharing food)

* Animal contact

* Recent hospitalization: associated with <u>health care-associated infections</u> (e.g., <u>C. difficile infection</u>)

* Medication use

* May cause medication-induced diarrhea

* Medications commonly associated with diarrhea include:  [[15]](/library/uMcpq10)

* <u>Broad-spectrum antibiotics</u> (especially <u>cephalosporins</u>)

* <u>Antacids</u> and <u>PPIs</u>

* <u>NSAIDs</u>

* <u>Metformin</u>

* <u>Colchicine</u>

* <u>Cholesterol</u>-lowering agents

* <u>Antineoplastic drugs</u>

* <u>Surgery</u> [[16]](/library/KLcUA10)

* <u>Cholecystectomy</u>  [[17]](/library/6LcjA10)

* <u>Bowel resection</u>: may cause <u>short bowel syndrome</u>  [[18]](/library/GMcBJ10)

* <u>Vagotomy</u>: induces rapid gastric emptying, which may disrupt the protective effect of <u>stomach acid</u> [[18]](/library/GMcBJ10)

* Gastric and/or esophageal <u>surgery</u>, e.g., <u>bariatric surgery</u>: may result in fat <u>malabsorption</u>, <u>SIBO</u>, or <u>dumping syndrome</u>

* <u>Radiation therapy</u>: may cause secondary enterocolitis  [[16]](/library/KLcUA10)





> [!TIP]
> More than 700 medications can cause diarrhea and, therefore, the introduction of a new medication within 6–8 weeks of the onset of diarrhea should be considered as a potential cause. [[15]](/library/uMcpq10)




> [!TIP]
> <u>Chronic diarrhea</u> is common after <u>bariatric surgery</u>. [[19]](/library/pocL1W0)[[20]](/library/Jocs1W0)




### Red flags in diarrhea [[21]](/library/fUakcP)[[22]](/library/kIYm1q)[[23]](/library/FMcgq10)[[24]](/library/tMcXq10)




* Acute or <u>persistent diarrhea</u>

* Symptoms of <u>inflammatory diarrhea</u> (<u>dysentery</u>)

* Systemic symptoms, e.g., <u>fever</u>, <u>hypotension</u>

* <u>Severe dehydration</u>

* Bloody stools

* Severe abdominal <u>pain</u>

* Patient characteristics that suggest an increased risk of severe disease

* Chronic illness or <u>immunocompromise</u>

* Age > 65 years

* Recent <u>antibiotic</u> use

* > 48 hours duration without improvement

* <u>Chronic diarrhea</u>

* <u>Hypoalbuminemia</u>

* Bloody stools

* Symptoms wake the patient from <u>sleep</u>

* <u>Unintended weight loss</u>

* <u>Family history</u> of GI cancer

* Symptom onset after 50 years of age

---

## Diagnostics

### General principles [[10]](/library/7Mc4J10)[[12]](/library/Sncys10)[[22]](/library/kIYm1q)[[25]](/library/J7Ys5q)




* <u>Acute diarrhea</u>

* Testing is not required in the majority of cases.

* Indications for testing include the presence of <u>red flags in diarrhea</u> and <u>risk factors</u> for specific etiologies.

* <u>Persistent diarrhea</u>: Testing is usually limited to stool studies for <u>infectious gastroenteritis</u>.

* <u>Chronic diarrhea</u>

* Testing is initially broad with advanced follow-up testing as indicated. [[21]](/library/fUakcP)[[25]](/library/J7Ys5q)

* Repeat stool testing for <u>infectious gastroenteritis</u>.





> [!TIP]
> Diagnostic testing is seldom indicated in <u>acute diarrhea</u> in the absence of <u>red flag symptoms</u>.




### Testing for diarrhea




For specific indications for testing, see the respective subsections below on acute, persistent, and <u>chronic diarrhea</u>.




* Blood tests

* <u>CBC</u>: To evaluate for <u>anemia</u>, <u>leukocytosis</u>, and/or <u>leukopenia</u>

* <u>CMP</u>: Assessment of <u>laboratory findings in dehydration</u> (e.g., <u>electrolyte</u> abnormalities, <u>AKI</u>) and/or <u>liver</u> disease

* <u>CRP</u>, <u>ESR</u>: <u>Markers of inflammation</u>

* <u>Blood cultures</u>: Identification of <u>bacteremia</u>

* Blood gases: Assessment of acid-base status

* <u>Celiac disease serology</u>: Initial testing for <u>celiac disease</u>

* Breath tests [[26]](/library/y9cdJe0)

* <u>Hydrogen breath test</u> (e.g., <u>glucose hydrogen breath test</u>, <u>lactose hydrogen breath test</u>): Diagnosis of <u>SIBO</u> and <u>carbohydrate</u> intolerance

* <u>C-D-xylose breath test</u>: Diagnosis of intestinal <u>malabsorption</u> and <u>SIBO</u>

* CT abdomen or <u>MRI</u> abdomen: Identification of inflammation, structural disease, and/or <u>ischemia</u> [[12]](/library/Sncys10)

* Endoscopic studies [[12]](/library/Sncys10)[[18]](/library/GMcBJ10)

* <u>Upper endoscopy</u> or <u>enteroscopy</u> with <u>biopsy</u> (± <u>aspiration</u>): Diagnosis of <u>mucosal</u> disease (e.g., <u>celiac disease</u>), infection, or <u>malignancy</u> in the <u>small intestine</u>

* <u>Colonoscopy</u> with <u>biopsies</u>: Diagnosis of inflammatory disease, infection, or <u>malignancy</u>





> [!TIP]
> Endoscopic studies have limited diagnostic value in <u>acute diarrhea</u> but are commonly needed for the workup of <u>chronic diarrhea</u> to evaluate for the presence of inflammatory or <u>neoplastic</u> diseases. Their utility in <u>persistent diarrhea</u> is uncertain.




#### Stool diagnostic studies




* Stool culture: can be indicated if <u>red flags in diarrhea</u> are present (e.g., suspected invasive <u>bacterial enteritis</u>)

* <u>Stool tests for CDI</u>: if <u>C. difficile infection</u> is suspected





| <u>Stool diagnostic studies</u> in diarrhea |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Suspected etiology | Test | Purpose |
| Infectious diseases | <u>Stool culture</u> | Identification of infectious agents (e.g., in <u>bacterial gastroenteritis</u>) |
| <u>Stool microscopy</u> | Visualization of <u>ova</u> or <u>parasites</u> in the stool |  |
| Culture-independent methods, e.g., <u>multiplex molecular diagnostic panel for diarrhea</u> (<u>PCR</u>) | Identification of infectious agents in bacterial, viral, and <u>protozoal</u> <u>gastroenteritis</u>  [[25]](/library/J7Ys5q)<br> |  |
| Quantitative culture of small intestinal <u>aspirate</u><br> | Used to diagnose <u>SIBO</u> (<u>gold standard test</u> for bacterial overgrowth) |  |
| <br><u>Stool tests for C. difficile infection</u> (e.g., toxin test) | Identification of <u>C. difficile infection</u><br> |  |
| Inflammation | <u>Stool microscopy</u> | Visualization of fecal <u>leukocytes</u><br> |
| <br><u>Fecal occult blood test</u> (<u>FOBT</u>) | To screen for <u>malignancy</u> and <u>mucosal</u> inflammation |  |
| <u>FIT DNA test</u> | To screen for <u>colonic</u> cancer and <u>adenomatous polyps</u><br> |  |
| <br><u>Fecal calprotectin</u> and <u>lactoferrin</u><br> | Markers of <u>inflammatory bowel disease</u> (<u>IBD</u>) |  |
| <u>Malabsorption</u> | <u>Sudan stain</u> | Qualitative test for <u>steatorrhea</u><br> |
| <u>72-hour quantitative fecal fat estimation</u> | Quantitative test for <u>steatorrhea</u><br> |  |
| <u>Fecal elastase-1</u> | Confirmation of <u>steatorrhea</u> due to <u>exocrine pancreatic insufficiency</u><br> |  |
| Stool <u>electrolytes</u> (e.g., Na<sup>+</sup>, <u>K<sup>+</sup></u>) | Used to calculate <u>stool osmotic gap</u><br> |  |
| Stool <u>pH</u><br> | Identification of <u>carbohydrate malabsorption</u> <br> |  |




* Stool osmotic gap [[11]](/library/HMcKJ10)[[16]](/library/KLcUA10)[[18]](/library/GMcBJ10)

* An equation used in patients with <u>watery diarrhea</u> to differentiate between osmotic, secretory, and <u>functional diarrhea</u>

* Calculation: 290 - [2 × (stool <u>sodium</u> + stool <u>potassium</u>)]

* Normal <u>stool osmotic gap</u>: 50–100 mOsm/kg




|  | Low <u>stool osmotic gap</u> | High <u>stool osmotic gap</u> |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Osmotic gap | <br>* < 50 mOsm/kg<br><br> | <br>* ≥ 100 mOsm/kg<br><br> |
| Interpretation | <br>* <u>Secretory diarrhea</u> (↑ secretion and/or inhibition of water absorption) or <u>functional diarrhea</u> (increased intestinal movement)<br><br> | <br>* <u>Osmotic diarrhea</u> (osmotic pull of ingested substances draws water into the intestinal lumen)<br><br> |
| Example causes | <br><br>* Foodborne infections (e.g., <u>Vibrio cholerae</u>, <u>enterotoxigenic E. coli</u>)<br><br>* Endocrine tumors (e.g., <u>VIPoma</u>, medullary <u>carcinoma</u> of the <u>thyroid</u>, <u>gastrinoma</u>)<br><br>* Impaired absorption of <u>bile acids</u> and/or salts (<u>bile acid diarrhea</u>)<br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Osmotic laxative</u> ingestion (e.g., <u>magnesium citrate</u>)<br><br>* <u>Malabsorption</u> (e.g., <u>celiac disease</u>, <u>Whipple disease</u>)<br><br>* <u>Pancreatic</u> insufficiency<br><br><br> |





> [!TIP]
> The loss of <u>bicarbonate</u>-rich fluid in severe diarrhea may cause nonanion gap <u>metabolic acidosis</u>.

---

## Supportive care

### <u>Dehydration and hypovolemia</u> [[21]](/library/fUakcP)




Therapy is guided by <u>clinical features of dehydration and hypovolemia</u> and <u>laboratory findings in dehydration and hypovolemia</u>.




* Mild to <u>moderate dehydration</u>: Start <u>oral rehydration therapy</u>, e.g., use <u>oral rehydration solution</u>.  [[21]](/library/fUakcP)

* Severe cases

* Start <u>IV fluid resuscitation</u> (e.g., with <u>normal saline</u>) and monitor <u>hemodynamic parameters</u>.

* Consider hospitalization.





> [!TIP]
> <u>Acute diarrhea</u> is usually a <u>self-limited</u> viral infection and management primarily supportive.




> [!WARNING]
> Early rehydration is especially important in children.




### Antidiarrheal agents [[16]](/library/KLcUA10)[[25]](/library/J7Ys5q)




* <u>Bismuth subsalicylate</u> DOSAGE  [[25]](/library/J7Ys5q)

* Converts to <u>bismuth</u> and <u>salicylic acid</u> in the <u>GI tract</u>

* Has antisecretory, antimicrobial, and antiinflammatory effects

* Can be used in bacterial diarrhea

* <u>Loperamide</u> DOSAGE ;  [[25]](/library/J7Ys5q)[[27]](/library/nLc7y10)[[28]](/library/fjck-X0)

* <u>Opioid</u> <u>receptor</u> <u>agonist</u> that increases <u>intestinal transit time</u>

* Best initial treatment for <u>chemotherapy-induced diarrhea</u>

* Cautions

* Should not be used for > 48 hours without reevaluation of the patient

* Should be avoided if the patient is <u>febrile</u> or has bloody stools (dysenteric diarrhea)

* Racecadotril (not available in the US) [[16]](/library/KLcUA10)[[29]](/library/jCc_7e0)

* Enkephalinase inhibitor that reduces the hypersecretion of <u>electrolytes</u> and water into the intestinal lumen

* Appears to be well-tolerated and effective in bacterial diarrhea





> [!WARNING]
> <u>Loperamide</u> should be avoided in patients with suspected invasive diarrhea with inflammatory features, as it reduces intestinal motility, which consequently increases the risk of bacterial <u>colonization</u> and invasion. [[30]](/library/_eY5Yo)

## Subtypes and variants

### Traveler's diarrhea [[36]](/library/VaaGjQ)[[37]](/library/hoccbW0)




* Definition: ≥ 3 unformed stools with at least one additional <u>enteric</u> symptom occurring after recent travel

* <u>Epidemiology</u>

* The highest rates occur after travel to Africa and South, Central, and West Asia.

* Approximately 25% of all travelers develop <u>traveler's diarrhea</u>.

* Etiology

* <u>Enterotoxigenic E. coli</u> (<u>ETEC</u>) is the most common cause of <u>traveler's diarrhea</u> globally.

* <u>Campylobacter jejuni</u> is the most common cause in Southeast Asia.

* Other pathogens

* Bacterial: <u>Shigella</u> spp., <u>Salmonella</u> spp., other <u>E. coli</u> strains (e.g., <u>EAEC</u>)

* Viral: <u>norovirus</u>, <u>rotavirus</u>, <u>astrovirus</u>

* <u>Protozoal</u>: <u>Giardia duodenalis</u>, <u>E. histolytica</u>

* Clinical features: <u>exudative</u>-inflammatory or <u>secretory diarrhea</u>, abdominal cramping, abdominal <u>pain</u>

* Antibiotics for traveler's diarrhea: Reserve for moderate to severe illness. [[25]](/library/J7Ys5q)[[32]](/library/ULcbC10)[[36]](/library/VaaGjQ)

* For most destinations: <u>ciprofloxacin</u> (<u>off label</u>) DOSAGE OR <u>rifaximin</u> DOSAGE  [[36]](/library/VaaGjQ)

* For travelers to South or Southeast Asia: <u>azithromycin</u> (<u>off label</u>) DOSAGE [[36]](/library/VaaGjQ)

* <u>Supportive care</u> [[25]](/library/J7Ys5q)

* Treatment for <u>dehydration</u> (e.g., <u>oral rehydration solution</u>)

* <u>Bismuth subsalicylate</u> for patients with mild to moderate illness

* <u>Loperamide</u> for patients receiving <u>antibiotic therapy</u> (can reduce the duration of illness)

* See “<u>Antidiarrheal agents</u>” for dosages.

* Postinfectious sequelae

* <u>Postinfectious IBS</u>: may occur in 3–20% of patients

* <u>Reactive arthritis</u>: may last months to years

* <u>Guillain-Barre syndrome</u>: may develop 1–4 weeks after infection (most commonly after <u>Campylobacter</u> infection)





> [!TIP]
> <u>Antibiotic</u> treatment is not recommended in patients with mild <u>traveler's diarrhea</u>.




> [!NOTE]
> <u>Bismuth subsalicylate</u> is an <u>antidiarrheal agent</u> used to treat <u>traveler's diarrhea</u> (caused by <u>enterotoxigenic Escherichia coli</u>).




#### Pharmacological prophylaxis for traveler's diarrhea [[25]](/library/J7Ys5q)[[36]](/library/VaaGjQ)




Consider for travelers to high-risk areas (under specialist guidance); options include:




* <u>Bismuth subsalicylate</u> (<u>off label</u>) DOSAGE [[25]](/library/J7Ys5q)[[36]](/library/VaaGjQ)[[38]](/library/3ocSbW0)

* Consider for travelers with no contraindications for use.

* Should be taken with meals and at bedtime

* <u>Antibiotic prophylaxis</u> (generally discouraged) :

* Consider short-term administration in travelers who are at high-risk for developing serious complications.

* Agents include <u>fluoroquinolones</u>, <u>azithromycin</u>, and <u>rifaximin</u>.

* Probiotics, prebiotics, and synbiotics are not recommended.





### Factitious diarrhea [[11]](/library/HMcKJ10)




* Definition: self-induced diarrhea, usually due to <u>laxative abuse</u> (often occurs in individuals with <u>factitious disorders</u>), or dilution of stools with solutions

* <u>Epidemiology</u>

* Most prevalent in women

* Patients are usually <u>health care professionals</u>.

* History of multiple hospital admissions

* Clinical features: <u>chronic diarrhea</u> without an identifiable cause

* Diagnostics

* Laboratory tests: <u>metabolic acidosis</u> , <u>metabolic alkalosis</u> , <u>hypokalemia</u>, <u>hypermagnesemia</u>

* Stool <u>osmolarity</u>

* < 290 mOsm/L: indicates dilution of the stool with a hypotonic solution

* > 600 mOsm/L: indicates dilution of the stool with a hypertonic solution

* <u>Laxative</u> screen [[18]](/library/GMcBJ10)

* <u>Colonoscopy</u>: may show <u>melanosis coli</u> in cases of anthraquinone  abuse

* Treatment

* Correction of <u>electrolyte</u> disturbances and <u>dehydration</u>

* Referral for <u>psychotherapy</u>





#### Laxative abuse




* Types of <u>laxative</u>

* Bulking agent: e.g., flaxseed

* <u>Osmotic laxatives</u>: e.g., <u>lactulose</u>, macrogols (<u>polyethylene glycol</u>), <u>magnesium sulfate</u>, <u>sodium</u> sulfate

* Diphenolic <u>laxatives</u>: <u>bisacodyl</u>, <u>sodium picosulfate</u>

* Anthraquinones: e.g., <u>senna</u>, aloe vera, rhubarb

* Clinical features

* <u>Osmotic diarrhea</u>, <u>meteorism</u>

* <u>Dehydration</u>

* <u>Hypokalemia</u>

* Melanosis coli: benign <u>hyperpigmentation</u> of the <u>colonic</u> <u>mucosa</u> caused by anthraquinone abuse  [[39]](/library/k_cmoU0)

* <u>Colonoscopy</u>: patches of dark brown pigmentation interspersed with pale <u>mucosa</u>

* <u>Biopsy</u>: <u>lipofuscin</u>-laden <u>macrophages</u> demonstrated on <u>periodic acid-Schiff</u> staining





![Melanosis coli](media/va8kf1dhuqzx8bjotvg87y3l.jpg)

Melanosis coli

![Melanosis coli in chronic laxative abuse](media/rl8924u0lj30p3p927nh0kt2.jpg)

Melanosis coli in chronic laxative abuse




### Bile acid diarrhea




* Definition: <u>secretory diarrhea</u> with or without <u>steatorrhea</u> due to increased <u>colonic</u> secretion and motility secondary to an increased concentration of <u>bile acids</u> within the <u>colon</u>

* <u>Epidemiology</u>: approx. 1% <u>global</u> <u>prevalence</u> [[40]](/library/rbWfEP0)

* Etiology

* <u>Ileal</u> dysfunction or decreased <u>bile acid</u> reabsorption in the <u>ileum</u> (e.g., due to <u>ileal</u> resection, <u>Crohn disease</u>)

* Postcholecystectomy

* Hepatic overproduction of <u>bile acids</u>

* <u>Biliary-enteric fistula</u>

* Clinical features

* Bowel frequency and urgency

* <u>Fecal incontinence</u>

* Abdominal cramping, abdominal <u>pain</u>

* Nocturnal <u>fecal urgency</u>

* <u>Bloating</u>, flatulence

* Management [[41]](/library/9YWNrP0)

* First-line: <u>bile</u>-acid sequestrants (e.g., <u>cholestyramine</u>, <u>colestipol</u>)

* Dietary intervention: low-fat diet
